# Week 2, Day 5.1 — TypeScript check-in: nothing new today

Day 5.2 splits one test into several and watches the second one fail. Nothing about that
needs new TypeScript — it's the same `test()`/`async ({ page })` shape you've written all
week. This lesson is a pointer, not a primer.

> **This day introduces no new TypeScript**, so there is no primer to work through. Go
> straight to [Day 5.2](/learn/w2/d5/p2).

## What today's code leans on

| Concept | Status | Where it was taught |
|---|---|---|
| `async ({ page }) => {}`, destructuring a fixture | already covered | [Week 1, Day 5.1](/learn/w1/d5/p1) |
| `test()`, `expect()`, the assertions gap | already covered | [Week 1, Day 5.2](/learn/w1/d5/p2) |
| `test.describe(...)` grouping | new **name** today, no new syntax — it's a function call around `test()`s you already know how to write | — |

The only thing Day 5.2 adds is a fact about how Playwright runs your tests, not a
language feature: **every `test()` gets its own fresh `page`.** That's the whole lesson.

## What's next

[Day 5.2 — Splitting one long test](/learn/w2/d5/p2) shows why that fact matters the moment
you split a test for readability.

parts.title: Splitting one long test, and the problem it creates

blocks.text:
# Week 2, Day 5.2 — Splitting one long test, and the problem it creates

By the end of this lesson you will have run one long test, split it into five small
ones, and watched a real failure appear that has nothing to do with a typo — it's
Playwright's central design decision showing up for the first time.

> **Mode: test-runner.** This part is about running specs with the Playwright test runner. The studio editor runs library code, so follow these along in your own checkout.

## One test, five things

A test that logs in, views transaction history, pays a bill, checks billing history, and
logs out reads fine — until it fails. When it does, the failure just says "this test
failed"; you're left guessing which of the five steps broke.

There's also a harder ceiling: **every Playwright test has a default budget of 30
seconds.** Each extra real step — a navigation, a slow render — eats into that budget,
and a test doing five things is five times more likely to bump into it than a test doing
one.

## Example 1 — the one long test, run for real

**Objective:** see the actual duration of a single test doing five real things.

> ▶ **Run it yourself too:** `npx playwright test week2/generated/day5-one-long-test.spec.ts`

**Expected result:** `1 passed`, in roughly 25–30 seconds — measured against the live
banking app while writing this lesson. That's already within a few seconds of the
default 30-second test timeout, for a journey that does nothing unusual.

Playwright's own reporter has a name for this: a **slow test file** warning appears when
a file's tests take a long time in total, suggesting you split them so they can run in
parallel. You've just watched a smaller version of that same pressure build inside a
single test.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Example 2 — split it, the obvious way

**Objective:** break the journey into small `test()`s — one per concern, the same
response to "each failure should name one thing" that [Day 1](/learn/w1/d5/p2)
already taught you to want from an assertion.

> ▶ **Run it yourself too:** `npx playwright test week2/generated/day5-split-isolation.spec.ts`

**Expected result (verified live, reproduced twice while writing this):** `1 failed, 1
passed`.

```
Error: expect(locator).toBeVisible() failed
Locator: getByText('Leela')
Expected: visible
Error: element(s) not found
```

Read `test 2` again — there's no bug in it. It goes to `/dashboard` and looks for the
name. The name just isn't there, because **`test 2` never logged in.** `test 1` did, but
that session didn't carry over.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Why: every test gets a fresh `page`

This isn't a quirk of this app — it's Playwright's central design decision. Each `test()`
receives its own `page`: a blank tab, no cookies, no storage, nothing carried over from
any other test. That's what makes tests safe to run in any order, in parallel, and
without one test's failure corrupting the next one's starting state.

The cost is the flip side of the benefit: state you *want* to keep — like being logged
in — has to be shared on purpose. Splitting a test for readability is exactly the moment
this becomes visible, because now you have two tests where you used to have a single
continuous story.

**What's next fixes this for real.** [Day 5.3](/learn/w2/d5/p3) previews the shape of the
fix; [Week 3, Day 2.1](/learn/w3/d2/p1) and
[Week 3, Day 2.2](/learn/w3/d2/p2) build it properly, with hooks named and
explained.

## Best practices

- Split a long test by concern — the readability win is real.
- Before you split, ask what state the later pieces need that only the earlier ones set
  up. Login is the most common one.
- Don't "fix" this by copy-pasting the login steps into every test — [Day 5.3](/learn/w2/d5/p3)
  shows why sharing beats repeating once you have more than two or three tests.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | What you see | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Splitting a long test without checking what state carries over | one or more of the new tests fail immediately | identify the shared setup, then read Day 5.3 |
| Assuming `toHaveURL(/dashboard/)` proves you're logged in | it doesn't — this app has no route guard, so a logged-out page still loads at that URL | assert on user-specific content instead (the name, an account number) |
| Re-running the whole login in every split test "just in case" | works, but every test pays the login cost again | fine for a couple of tests; Day 5.3 previews the alternative once it doesn't scale |

## What's next

[Day 5.3](/learn/w2/d5/p3) previews the fix — not the full lesson, that's week3's job.

parts.title: Preview: the shape of the fix

blocks.text:
# Week 2, Day 5.3 — Preview: the shape of the fix

**This lesson does not teach hooks.** It shows the fix from Day 5.2 running for real,
names the pieces, and points you at where each one is actually explained.

> **Mode: test-runner.** This part is about running specs with the Playwright test runner. The studio editor runs library code, so follow these along in your own checkout.

## The shape, named but not explained

| Piece | What it's for |
|---|---|
| `browser.newContext()` | a fresh, isolated environment you create yourself — instead of one being created per test automatically |
| `test.beforeAll(...)` | runs once, before the first test in a group — where you'd create that shared context and log in |
| `test.afterAll(...)` | runs once, after the last test — where you'd close it |
| `test.describe(...)` | groups the tests that share that context |
| `test.describe.configure({ mode: "serial" })` | tells Playwright these tests depend on each other and must not run at the same time |

All five names come from [Week 3, Day 2.1](/learn/w3/d2/p1) (the TypeScript
underneath them — arrow functions passed as hook bodies) and
[Week 3, Day 2.2](/learn/w3/d2/p2) (what each one actually does, and why). This
lesson only proves the shape works.

## Watching it work

**Objective:** the exact two tests from Day 5.2 — Example 2 — passing this time, because
they share one login instead of each getting a blank page.

> ▶ **Run it yourself too:** `npx playwright test week2/generated/day5-shared-context-preview.spec.ts`

**Expected result:** `2 passed` — verified live while writing this lesson.

One measured detail worth keeping, even at preview depth: `test 2` doesn't call
`page.goto()` again. This app keeps its session **in memory only** (no cookies, no
`localStorage`) — a full navigation reloads the page and wipes it, whether or not the
context is shared. Sharing the context gets you the same tab still sitting where test 1
left it; it doesn't survive a fresh `goto()` any more than an isolated one would.

## What's next

[Week 3, Day 2.1](/learn/w3/d2/p1) and [Week 3, Day 2.2](/learn/w3/d2/p2)
build this properly: why `page` and `browser` have different scope, all four hooks
explained, `test.describe` grouping, and when to reach for `mode: "serial"`. This preview
stops here on purpose — that's next week's first lesson, not this lesson's.

blocks.text:
# Week 2, Day 5.4 — Practice: splitting tests, and the isolation problem

Three problems. The third one has no code to write — it's a question, because the real
hook lesson is week3's job, not this lesson's.

Start in a fresh cell in this lesson. When a problem asks for a spec file, write it
into `week2/generated/` and run it with `npx playwright test`.

## End of week 2

Locators (role, placeholder, XPath, CSS, the sibling axis), real assertions, unique test
data, and the isolation problem a split test creates are all in hand now. week3 starts
immediately with the fix — hooks — and then configuration.

problems.statement:
**What to build.** Pick a different two-step scenario on the banking app (for example:
test 1 navigates to Pay Bills and reads a value; test 2 tries to read something from
Billing History that assumes test 1 already put you there) and reproduce the isolation
failure yourself — two `test()`s in one `describe`, the second assuming state from the
first.

**Where.** A spec in `week2/generated/`.

**How you will know it worked.** The second test fails with a real Playwright error, not
a typo of yours — and you can explain in one sentence why it's failing.

> **Hint** — Day 5.2, Example 2 is the template. Change *what* state test 2 assumes, not
> the shape.

**What to build.** Fix the spec you just wrote using `browser.newContext()` — the same
shape from [Day 5.3](/learn/w2/d5/p3) — and confirm both tests now pass.

**Where.** The same spec file, or a new one in `week2/generated/`.

**How you will know it worked.** `2 passed`, where a moment ago it was `1 failed, 1
passed`.

Day 5.3 named five pieces: `browser.newContext()`, `test.beforeAll`, `test.afterAll`,
`test.describe`, and `mode: "serial"`.

**Question:** if you wanted that shared context built exactly **once** for every test in
a whole spec file — not re-created per test — which single hook name from that list is
the one doing that job, and why does it have to be the one that runs *before the first
test*, rather than one that runs before *each* test?

Write your answer as a comment in a cell below. There's no code to run here — check
your reasoning against [Week 3, Day 2.2](/learn/w3/d2/p2) once you get there.
problems.stub: // Problem 3 — your reasoning here, as a comment. No code to run.
problems.solution:
**The answer: `test.beforeAll`.**

> `test.beforeAll` runs **once per file**, before any test in it. So a context created inside it is built exactly once and every test in the file shares it. `test.beforeEach` would run before *each* test and rebuild the context every time — which is the per-test isolation you already get for free, at the cost of a login on every test.

**Where the other four sit:**

| Piece | What it does |
|---|---|
| `browser.newContext()` | Creates the shared session. It is *what* is shared. |
| **`test.beforeAll`** | Runs it **once**. It is *why* it is shared rather than rebuilt. |
| `test.afterAll` | Closes it once, at the end. Without this the context leaks. |
| `test.describe` | Groups the tests so "once per file" has a scope, and gives the block a name in the report. |
| `mode: "serial"` | Stops them running in parallel and fighting over the one page. |

**The distinction worth holding on to.** `beforeAll` is about *how often setup runs*; `mode: "serial"` is about *whether tests may overlap*. They are easy to conflate because a shared context needs both, but they answer different questions — and in Week 3, when you meet hooks properly, you will use each of them without the other.

> `afterAll` is the one people leave out. It costs nothing on a two-test file and quietly exhausts a CI runner on a large suite.
